analysis.one_liner: Appropriates $1 billion in U.S. taxpayer money to buy Israel an Iron Dome missile defense system.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have sent $1 billion of U.S. taxpayer money to Israel for Iron Dome missiles, was referred to the House Appropriations Committee and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take $1 billion out of the Treasury and give it to Israel's government to buy Iron Dome missile defense batteries, the system used to shoot down short-range rockets. The money would be in addition to what the U.S. already provides under an existing purchase agreement, and it would be justified as replacing missiles used up during a recent round of fighting in Gaza. The bill went to the House Appropriations Committee the day it was introduced and was never acted on again before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The government of Israel would receive $1 billion worth of Iron Dome missile defense equipment paid for by U.S. taxpayers. The American defense contractors that build Iron Dome interceptors and components would gain the manufacturing work. Israeli civilians living under short-range rocket threat would benefit from a replenished defensive shield.

how_it_helps.text: The bill appropriates $1 billion for the Department of Defense to hand to the government of Israel to buy Iron Dome missile defense batteries.
The funding is aimed at countering short-range rocket threats and is tied to replenishing systems used in a recent round of fighting between Israel and armed groups in Gaza.
The money would be in addition to amounts already provided under the existing U.S.-Israel Iron Dome Procurement Agreement, adding new funds on top of prior appropriations.

analysis.who_pays: U.S. taxpayers, through $1 billion in new federal spending with no offset, and ultimately federal borrowers, since the money would be appropriated out of the general Treasury with no corresponding cuts or revenue.

drawbacks.text: The $1 billion would come directly out of the Treasury with no offsetting spending cuts or new revenue, adding to federal deficits.

The money would go to a foreign government's weapons procurement rather than to domestic programs, and the bill text names an existing military operation as the justification rather than a fresh authorization or debate.
The funds would remain available until September 30, 2024, a multi-year window with no reporting or oversight requirements written into the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's purpose — replenishing Israel's short-range missile defenses after rocket attacks — is one that many in both parties support, and no one in the record opposed it on the merits. The cost is $1 billion drawn from the Treasury with no spending offset and no audit provisions in the text, and the money would primarily flow to a foreign government and the contractors that build the system rather than to any domestic need. The bill was never weighed against alternatives because it never got a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Appropriations Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Jacobs introduced the bill on September 21, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Appropriations.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote at any point in the 117th Congress.
The bill died in committee when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and any bill not passed by then must start over from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: U.S. taxpayers kept the $1 billion, since the bill never moved. Defense contractors and the Israeli government did not receive the additional funds, and no member had to take a recorded vote on the spending.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: U.S. taxpayers, who kept the $1 billion

for.name: 10 House Republicans
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Buchanan, Weber, Gohmert, McKinley, Franklin, Mann, Garbarino, and Zeldin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Appropriations
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over spending bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 21, 2021 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill died in the Democratically controlled Appropriations Committee without ever coming to a vote.

industries.industry: Defense contractors (Iron Dome manufacturers, including Raytheon as the U.S. workshare partner)
industries.note: An additional $1 billion in U.S. government procurement money for Iron Dome interceptors flows to the companies that build and supply the system. For ordinary people the cost is $1 billion in tax spending, not a direct price increase.

industries.industry: Foreign military assistance recipients (Government of Israel)
industries.note: Israel's military would receive $1 billion in U.S.-funded missile defense equipment at no cost to its own budget. This is one of the largest single-country recipients of U.S. defense dollars getting an additional appropriation.

The $1 billion would come out of general Treasury funds with no offset, meaning federal borrowing or forgoing other uses of that money. Citizens bear the cost with no direct domestic benefit specified in the bill.
